dimension: Postgres schema, indexing and storage efficiency (live production qztcgryhoanennsizcll)
summary: The schema itself is not the problem — it is over-indexed and over-built, but its storage footprint is trivial. Two facts reframe this dimension. First, the headline "481 unused indexes" is nearly worthless as a storage target: only 329 are safely droppable and they total 4.9 MB. The real cost of those indexes is write amplification on tables that take 400k+ inserts. Second, 86 MB of a 240 MB database (36%) is bloat and unpruned history in two tables nobody reads — net._http_response holds 15 kB of live data in 40 MB on disk, and cron.job_run_details holds 101 days of run logs for a single cron job. Separately, three genuinely missing indexes are measurable right now on live data: the job-queue tick query costs 1,614 ms because no index covers GROUP BY type, an email delivery-webhook UPDATE sequentially scans 47,036 rows on every call, and the email retry scan has burned 17 minutes of cumulative DB time. Column type waste was checked and is effectively absent (4 numeric columns on one 269-row table; no unbounded varchar, no timestamp-without-timezone) — I am reporting that as a negative result rather than padding. Stats have accumulated since 2026-04-30, so "never scanned" here means never scanned in four months, not merely young.

findings.title: net._http_response holds 15 kB of live data in 40 MB on disk and has absorbed 476 GB of buffer traffic
findings.evidence: SELECT pg_size_pretty(sum(pg_column_size(r.*))::bigint), pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('net._http_response')), count(*) FROM net._http_response r; => live_data='15 kB', on_disk='40 MB', rows=72. pg_class: relpages=5075, reltuples=72. pg_statio_user_tables: heap_blks_read=3830, heap_blks_hit=62342042 => 62,345,872 blocks x 8 kB = 476 GB of heap block traffic. pg_stat_user_tables: seq_scan=34365 on a 5,075-page relation. autovacuum has run exactly once ever (autovacuum_count=1, last_autovacuum='2026-08-05'), and n_dead_tup=0 so it will never run again — plain VACUUM cannot return the non-trailing free pages to the OS. NOTE: I falsified my first hypothesis — EXPLAIN DELETE FROM net._http_response WHERE created < now() - interval '6 hours' returns a Bitmap Index Scan on _http_response_created_idx, NOT a seq scan, so the bloat is not what makes the established cleanup DELETEs slow. The cost lands on the 34,365 sequential scans, each of which must walk the full page count regardless of finding ~29 rows.
findings.impact: 40 MB (17% of the 240 MB database) permanently occupied by empty pages, and 476 GB of buffer-cache traffic to serve a table whose entire live contents fit in two pages. A compacted relation would reduce that traffic by roughly three orders of magnitude. This is the storage-and-IO mechanism underneath the already-established pg_net cleanup cost, but it attaches to the seq-scan path, not the DELETE path.
findings.recommendation: VACUUM FULL net._http_response (needs table ownership — on Supabase this is a support request or a superuser-equivalent session; it takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock but the table is 72 rows so it will complete near-instantly). Then lower pg_net's response TTL so the relation cannot regrow, and schedule a periodic compaction. Do not attempt to fix this by tuning the DELETE — the DELETE is already using its index correctly.

findings.title: The job-queue tick query has no covering index and costs 1,614 ms per call because GROUP BY type forces a heap fetch for every pending row
findings.evidence: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT type, MAX(priority) FROM job_queue WHERE status='pending' AND run_at<=NOW() GROUP BY type; => 'Index Scan using idx_job_queue_pick ... Index Cond: (run_at <= now()) ... rows=18817 ... Buffers: shared hit=10332 dirtied=4 ... Execution Time: 1614.494 ms'. The index it picks is 'CREATE INDEX idx_job_queue_pick ON public.job_queue USING btree (priority DESC, run_at) WHERE (status = 'pending'::text)' — it contains neither `type` nor enough ordering to answer the aggregate, so all 18,817 matching rows are fetched from the heap. pg_stat_user_indexes confirms the pathology: idx_job_queue_pick has idx_scan=50701 but idx_tup_read=176296858, i.e. 3,478 index tuples read per scan. pg_statio_user_tables: job_queue heap_blks_hit=99266160 => 757 GB of heap block traffic, the largest of any table.
findings.impact: This is the single most expensive statement already banked by the lead (3,724,750 ms over 4,127 calls, mean 902 ms, max 3.1 s). The 1,614 ms I measured live is entirely avoidable: every column the query needs (type, priority, run_at, status) can live in one partial index, making this an index-only scan over ~200 pages instead of 10,332 buffer accesses.
findings.recommendation: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_job_queue_tick ON job_queue (type, priority DESC, run_at) WHERE status = 'pending'; This makes the tick an index-only scan. Keep idx_job_queue_pick — it still serves the actual job-claim path. Re-measure with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) after creation; expect sub-10 ms, which would return roughly an hour of cumulative exec time.

findings.title: email_logs.provider_message_id has no index — the delivery-webhook UPDATE sequentially scans all 47,036 rows on every call
findings.evidence: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT id FROM email_logs WHERE provider_message_id = 'no-such-id-control-probe'; => 'Seq Scan on email_logs ... Rows Removed by Filter: 47036 ... Buffers: shared hit=1792 ... Execution Time: 718.031 ms'. pg_stat_statements: 'UPDATE email_logs SET status=$2, sent_at=COALESCE(sent_at, NOW()) WHERE provider_message_id=$1' — calls=1063, total_exec_time=19316 ms, mean=18.2 ms, shared_blks_hit=1432948 (1,348 blocks per call). The six indexes on email_logs are on id, (group_id, created_at DESC), status, "to", template_key, and a partial (reference_type, reference_id) — none covers provider_message_id. Cardinality check: SELECT count(*), count(DISTINCT provider_message_id) FROM email_logs WHERE provider_message_id IS NOT NULL => 524 and 524, i.e. perfectly selective.
findings.impact: Every inbound email delivery-status webhook does a full table scan of a 14 MB table to update one row. Cost grows linearly with email_logs, which has no retention, so this silently gets worse forever. Currently 19.3 s of cumulative exec time and 1.4 M block hits for 1,063 updates that should each touch ~4 pages.
findings.recommendation: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_email_logs_provider_message_id ON email_logs (provider_message_id) WHERE provider_message_id IS NOT NULL; All 524 non-null values are distinct so the unique constraint is safe and also documents the intent. Index size will be ~24 kB.

findings.title: email_logs has no (status, created_at) index — the retry scan has burned 17 minutes of cumulative DB time using the wrong index
findings.evidence: pg_stat_statements: 'SELECT * FROM email_logs WHERE status = $1 AND created_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL $2 AND created_at <= NOW() - INTERVAL $3 ORDER BY created_at ASC LIMIT $4' — calls=27842, total_exec_time=1017658 ms (17.0 min), mean=36.6 ms, rows=199857, shared_blks_hit=2865885. Live plan: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) with status='failed' and a 7-day window => 'Index Scan using idx_email_logs_group_id ... Index Cond: (created_at >= ...) AND (created_at <= ...) ... Filter: ((status)::text = 'failed') ... Rows Removed by Filter: 2346 ... rows=5920 ... Sort Method: top-N heapsort ... Buffers: shared hit=2344 ... Execution Time: 969.847 ms'. The planner is forced onto idx_email_logs_group_id (group_id, created_at DESC), whose leading column is not constrained, then discards non-matching statuses and sorts. pg_stat_user_tables also shows email_logs seq_scan=1383 with seq_tup_read=37565499 (27,162 rows per scan).
findings.impact: 17 minutes of cumulative DB time, 2.87 M block hits, and a 969 ms worst-case for a query that a correct index answers by reading the first 50 index entries and stopping (the LIMIT would terminate the scan immediately, and the sort disappears because the index is already in created_at order). Compounding waste: this query feeds email_retry_failed, which the lead established is a DEAD job type (4,301 pending, last success 2026-08-20) — so this is expensive work in service of a job that never completes.
findings.recommendation: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_email_logs_status_created_at ON email_logs (status, created_at); Then re-check the plan — it should become a plain forward index scan with no Sort node and no Filter. Fix or retire the dead email_retry_failed job separately; the index is worth adding regardless because the same shape serves any status-plus-time-window scan.

findings.title: cron.job_run_details is 46 MB of unread, unpruned, never-vacuumed history for a single cron job
findings.evidence: SELECT min(start_time), max(start_time), count(*), sum(pg_column_size(job_run_details.*)) FROM cron.job_run_details; => oldest='2026-05-25 23:50:00', newest='2026-09-04 07:45:00', rows=29184, live_data='16 MB' against on_disk='46 MB' => 65.8% waste. pg_stat_user_tables: vacuum_count=0, autovacuum_count=0, last_autovacuum NULL, last_autoanalyze NULL, seq_scan=5, idx_scan=0. pg_class: relpages=0, reltuples=-1 (never analyzed). SELECT jobid, schedule, jobname FROM cron.job; returns exactly one row: jobid=2, schedule='*/5 * * * *', jobname='kitabuyetu-every-5-min' — 288 runs/day x 101 days = 29,088, matching the row count.
findings.impact: 46 MB (19% of the 240 MB database) for an audit trail of one cron job that nothing has ever read — its only index has zero scans and the table has been sequentially scanned 5 times in four months. pg_cron does not prune this table by default, so it grows ~460 kB/day, roughly 165 MB/year, forever.
findings.recommendation: Truncate or age it out — DELETE FROM cron.job_run_details WHERE end_time < now() - interval '7 days', then VACUUM FULL cron.job_run_details to return the 30 MB of bloat. Add a second pg_cron entry to run that DELETE nightly so it stays bounded. Nothing reads this table, so retention can be aggressive.

findings.title: The prior audit's unindexed-FK remediation (migration 121) is 93% waste: 56 of its 60 indexes have never been scanned
findings.evidence: docs/audits/DB_PERFORMANCE_ADVISOR_AUDIT_2026-08.md F2 reported 60 unindexed FKs and prescribed 'a single additive migration, CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS per column'. supabase/migrations/20260806050000_121_index_unindexed_foreign_keys.sql implements exactly that (61 CREATE INDEX statements, applied 2026-08-06). Joining those 60 index names against pg_stat_user_indexes today: created_and_present=60, never_scanned=56, used=4, total_scans_across_all_60=811, total_size='784 kB'. My own unindexed-FK check confirms the linter complaint was resolved — only 6 FK columns remain uncovered (sms_credit_ledger.created_by, sms_credit_ledger.payment_id, sms_credits.package_id, organization_subscriptions.assigned_by, sms_opt_outs.actor_id, investment_expenses.recorded_by), all on tables of 0-73 rows.
findings.impact: Sixty B-trees are now maintained on every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE to their tables, and 56 of them have returned nothing in a month of production. This is the largest single identifiable contributor to the unused-index population, and it was created by acting on an advisor lint rather than on observed query behaviour. It also explains why the earlier audit's own caveat (F4: 'the 296 unused index findings are not trustworthy... contaminated by brand-new tables') has now inverted — these indexes are no longer new, and they are genuinely dead.
findings.recommendation: Do not index FK columns reflexively. Drop the 56 never-scanned ones from migration 121 (they are plain non-unique indexes, so dropping is safe and reversible), and leave the 6 remaining unindexed FKs alone — every one of them is on a table with under 100 rows where a sequential scan is cheaper than an index. Revisit only if a specific join or cascade-delete shows up in pg_stat_statements.

findings.title: job_logs has no retention at all and its 11 MB primary key index has never been used
findings.evidence: job_logs is the largest application table: 131,666 rows, 58 MB total (31 MB heap + 26 MB indexes), oldest row 2026-08-02 — i.e. 33 days of data at ~4,000 rows/day. lib/jobs/db.ts:259-267 defines the only prune routine: 'export async function pruneOldJobs(days = 30)' whose body is 'DELETE FROM job_queue WHERE status IN ('completed','failed') AND updated_at < NOW() - ...' — it targets job_queue only. Searching the repo for any delete/cleanup/retention/purge/prune touching job_logs returns zero matches across app, lib, scripts and supabase/migrations. Separately, pg_stat_user_indexes shows job_logs_pkey with idx_scan=0 at 11 MB, while idx_job_logs_job_id (15 MB) carries all 153,436 scans.
findings.impact: 58 MB and growing on a trajectory of roughly 640 MB/year, in a 240 MB database, for debug logs nobody prunes. The 11 MB primary key is dead weight maintained on all 448,738 inserts — nothing has ever looked a job_log up by its own id in four months.
findings.recommendation: Extend pruneOldJobs to delete job_logs older than the same retention window (or shorter — 7 days is generous for job debug output), and call it from the same cleanup job. Consider whether job_logs needs a synthetic uuid primary key at all; if the table is only ever read by job_id, the PK is pure overhead, though dropping it is a larger change than it looks and should be weighed against the 11 MB it costs.

findings.title: Twelve pairs of exactly-duplicate indexes — same columns, same predicate — are maintained on every write
findings.evidence: Self-join of pg_index on (indrelid, indkey, indpred) restricted to schema public. Twelve pairs have byte-identical column lists and identical predicates, each a redundant plain index shadowing a unique/PK index that already covers it: billing_accounts_group_unique vs idx_billing_accounts_group_id; uq_cycle_number vs idx_cycles_group; member_mfa_secrets_pkey vs idx_mfa_secrets_member; members_phone_unique vs idx_members_phone; members_email_unique vs idx_members_email; mpesa_b2b_transactions_originator_conversation_id_key vs idx_b2b_originator; mpesa_b2c_transactions_originator_conversation_id_key vs idx_b2c_originator; mpesa_stk_requests_checkout_request_id_key vs idx_stk_checkout_req; organization_sms_credits_payment_id_key vs idx_org_sms_credits_payment_id; sms_credits_payment_id_key vs idx_sms_credits_payment_id; sms_delivery_reports_provider_msg_unique vs idx_dlr_msg_id (idx_scan=0 while the unique index has 25,829 scans); sms_group_settings_unique vs idx_sms_group_settings_group. The same query also surfaces ~30 narrower indexes fully prefix-covered by a wider index on the same table, all with idx_scan=0 (e.g. idx_group_members_group_id, shadowed by group_members_unique plus five other (group_id, x) composites).
findings.impact: Twenty-four B-trees where twelve would do, on tables including members, mpesa_stk_requests and sms_delivery_reports. Storage is negligible (mostly 8-16 kB each) but every INSERT and non-HOT UPDATE pays to maintain both copies, and each duplicate adds a candidate the planner must consider. sms_delivery_reports is the clearest case: 19,338 updates against 118 rows, with 7 indexes of which 4 are unused.
findings.recommendation: Drop the non-unique half of each of the twelve pairs — the unique/PK index serves every query the plain one could, so this is behaviour-preserving. Then drop the ~30 prefix-covered indexes that also have idx_scan=0. Confirm each is non-unique before dropping (a unique index may be enforcing a constraint even at zero scans).

findings.title: Default autovacuum thresholds leave 64 tables permanently unvacuumed and the planner structurally blind on 34
findings.evidence: SELECT relname, reloptions FROM pg_class WHERE relkind='r' AND reloptions IS NOT NULL; returns zero rows — no table anywhere has per-table autovacuum tuning. Cluster settings: autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor=0.2, autovacuum_vacuum_threshold=50, autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor=0.1, autovacuum_analyze_threshold=50. So a table needs 50 + 0.2*n_live dead tuples to be vacuumed and 50 + 0.1*n_live changes to be analyzed — thresholds a 9-row or 37-row table can essentially never reach. Counts: 64 public tables with rows have vacuum_count=0 and last_autovacuum NULL; 52 have analyze_count=0 AND autoanalyze_count=0; of those, 34 have pg_class.reltuples = -1 (never analyzed, planner has no estimate at all) and 14 more carry stale underestimates. Worst example: `groups` — reltuples=3 against n_live_tup=9, n_dead_tup=16, seq_scan=68717, seq_tup_read=354645, 1,007 MB of heap block traffic, last_autoanalyze NULL. Also `subscriptions` (planner 5 vs actual 11), `journal_entries` (12 vs 29), `payment_requests` (7 vs 21).
findings.impact: This is the mechanism behind the already-established never-vacuumed tables (group_members at 67.6% dead, groups, welfare_requests, credit_scores) — it is not a transient state that will resolve itself, it is a permanent consequence of default thresholds on small tables. The compounding effect is planning, not just bloat: 34 tables give the planner no row estimate whatsoever, which is how a 9-row table ends up on the hot path of 68,717 sequential scans.
findings.recommendation: Set per-table autovacuum storage parameters on the small hot tables so the thresholds are reachable, e.g. ALTER TABLE groups SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.0, autovacuum_vacuum_threshold = 20, autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor = 0.0, autovacuum_analyze_threshold = 20); applied to groups, group_members, members, welfare_requests, subscriptions, journal_entries, payment_requests and the other small-but-queried tables. Run a one-off ANALYZE across the public schema immediately to clear the 34 blind tables — that costs nothing and is safe on production.

findings.title: 55 of 144 public tables have never had a single row inserted, carrying 283 indexes, 105 RLS policies, 145 foreign keys and 27 triggers
findings.evidence: SELECT ... FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE schemaname='public' AND n_live_tup=0 AND n_tup_ins=0 => 55 tables, total size 2,640 kB; joined against pg_index/pg_policy/pg_trigger/pg_constraint: 283 indexes, 105 policies (of the 276 total in public), 27 non-internal triggers, 145 FK constraints. Worst offenders by index count on an empty table: payment_reallocations (15 indexes, 25 columns), share_transactions (14), mpesa_b2c_transactions (12), disbursement_requests (10), dividend_allocations (10). Cross-checking against code (ripgrep over app, lib, components, hooks, scripts, types, excluding tests/node_modules — control-verified: job_queue=8 refs, sms_usage_logs=20 refs) only four have zero application references anywhere: contact_submissions, newsletter_subscribers, platform_billing, platform_notifications. A fifth candidate, share_certificate_counters, has no app reference but IS referenced by the database function allocate_share_certificate_serial — confirmed via pg_proc.prosrc, so it is not dead.
findings.impact: 38% of the schema is inert. Storage is negligible (2.6 MB) but the maintenance tax is real and recurring: migrations 068, 096, 120, 122 and 131 all had to touch contact_submissions and platform_notifications to fix FK indexes, role literals and RLS policies on tables that have never held data. 105 of the 276 RLS policies guard empty tables. This inflates every schema-wide audit, every type-generation run, and every policy sweep.
findings.recommendation: Drop the four confirmed-dead tables (contact_submissions, newsletter_subscribers, platform_billing, platform_notifications) — zero rows, zero code references, zero DB-function references. Leave the other 51 alone: they back features that are built but unexercised, and dropping them would be a product decision, not an optimization. Do not drop share_certificate_counters. Going forward, exclude zero-insert tables from blanket remediation migrations so they stop consuming maintenance effort.

findings.title: The 481-unused-index figure is not a storage opportunity — only 4.9 MB is actually droppable
findings.evidence: SELECT count(*), count(*) FILTER (WHERE indisprimary), count(*) FILTER (WHERE indisunique AND NOT indisprimary), count(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT indisunique), pg_size_pretty(sum(pg_relation_size(indexrelid)) FILTER (WHERE NOT indisunique)) FROM pg_stat_user_indexes JOIN pg_index USING (indexrelid) WHERE schemaname='public' AND idx_scan=0; => total=479, primary_keys=98, unique_constraints=52, plain_droppable=329, plain_droppable_size='4872 kB'. Across all schemas: 926 indexes, 593 unused, 20 MB. The three largest droppable ones are idx_email_logs_template_key (600 kB, 0 scans), idx_reconciliations_date (472 kB, 0 scans) and idx_reconciliations_group (344 kB, 0 scans) — together 1.4 MB, with the remaining 326 mostly at the 8-16 kB single-page minimum. Also near-dead: idx_email_logs_to (640 kB, 2 scans in four months) and idx_mpesa_reconciliations_initiated_by (13 scans but idx_tup_read=35505, i.e. it reads the entire table each time — zero selectivity).
findings.impact: None directly, but the framing matters: 150 of the 479 are primary keys and unique constraints that must not be dropped, and the entire remaining set is worth under 5 MB against a 240 MB database. Treating '481 unused indexes' as a storage-reclamation project would spend real effort for ~2% of the database while the actual 86 MB sits in net._http_response and cron.job_run_details.
findings.recommendation: Target unused indexes for write amplification, not bytes — prioritise the ones on high-churn tables (email_logs at 47k inserts + 44k updates, and the 56 dead indexes from migration 121) and ignore the long tail of 16 kB stubs on empty tables. Drop idx_email_logs_template_key, idx_email_logs_to, idx_reconciliations_date and idx_reconciliations_group first: they sit on the two largest churning tables and cost the most per write.
